name: Pheromone sprays (Human Pheromone Sciences)

lead: Pheromone sprays are commercial fragrance products sold on the claim that they contain human sex pheromones that raise the wearer's attractiveness. Human Pheromone Sciences is named as a seller of such products.

Proponents say the compounds signal attraction. Researchers report that no pheromonal substance has been shown in peer-reviewed studies to directly influence human behavior, and describe the field as speculative and controversial. The studies in the entry's source search concern insect pheromones, not humans.

paras: Buyers apply the spray like a cologne or add it to their usual scent, usually before social outings or dates. Users judge results by the reactions they perceive.
No specific harms were found in the sources reviewed; as with any fragrance, skin irritation or allergy is possible. The main concern cited is that the attraction effect has not been demonstrated.

angle.text: Buyers spray these products hoping the claimed pheromones make them seem more attractive to others. Peer-reviewed research has not shown that human pheromones change behavior, so the effect rests on marketing and anecdote.

lead: Pheromone sprays are commercial fragrance products marketed as containing human sex pheromones that make the wearer more attractive to others. Human Pheromone Sciences is named as a seller of such products, and people use them in the way they use colognes and body sprays: applied before meeting people, in the hope that scent will increase attraction.[1]

The idea draws on research into chemical signals in animals and on small studies of compounds such as androstenol and androstadienone in humans. Wikipedia reports that no pheromonal substance has been shown in a peer-reviewed study to directly influence human behavior, and describes the field as one with small samples, publication bias and mixed results.[1]

Studies found under the term pheromone spray concern insects, such as microencapsulated sex pheromone sprays used on codling moths and queen pheromone sprays used on honey bee crops, rather than human products.[2][3]
infobox: No peer-reviewed human study has shown a pheromone directly influences behavior[1]

paras: Pheromone sprays are colognes, body sprays and similar fragrance products marketed as containing human sex pheromones that make the wearer more attractive. Human Pheromone Sciences is named as a seller of such products. Users apply them as they would any scent before meeting people, treating scent as one more layer of grooming alongside clothing, skincare and cologne [1].

Peter Karlson and Martin Lüscher coined the word pheromone in 1959 for chemical signals passed between members of one species that trigger innate behaviours. The idea built on Adolf Butenandt's isolation of bombykol, the silkworm sex attractant, and pheromones are now studied across organisms from bacteria to insects [1].

Martha McClintock's 1971 Nature paper reported that women's menstrual cycles could shift in response to sweat odours from other women, the so-called McClintock effect. Later work has questioned whether menstrual synchrony occurs, and methodological doubts have been raised [1].

A 1978 study by Kirk-Smith and colleagues had participants wear masks treated with androstenol and rate photographs; those exposed rated the pictures as warmer and friendlier [1]. A 1983 study reported that androstenone changed skin conductance [1]. In a study by Hummer and McClintock, androstadienone applied to the upper lip of 50 men and women shifted attention toward emotional facial expressions, with women responding more positively and men more negatively [1]. A 2019 study by Oren and colleagues reported that a putative pheromone affected men's sexual cognition, though Wikipedia's account does not show a replication [1].

Five axillary steroids have been proposed as human pheromones: androstadienol, androstadienone, androstenol, androstenone and androsterone. Wikipedia reports that none of the three best-known, androstadienone, androstenone and androstenol, has been rigorously proven to act as a pheromone [1]. Studies of vaginal fatty acids in rhesus monkeys, called copulins, have also been discussed, though human ovulation is concealed and the compounds may serve other purposes [1].

In many animals the vomeronasal organ detects pheromones. In humans its receptor genes are nonfunctional pseudogenes and the organ appears atrophied or absent in adults, so how chemicals reach the brain is disputed. Six trace amine-associated receptors are expressed in the human olfactory epithelium, but their function is unclear [1]. Separate studies on major histocompatibility complex profiles found that people's chosen artificial odours and preferences for others' body odour were partly shaped by MHC type [1].

Reviewers including Hays (2003) and Wyatt (2003), and a neuroscience textbook by Bear and colleagues (2006), note the absence of peer-reviewed evidence for human sexual-attraction pheromones. A 2016 BBC article concluded that pheromones are probably not why people find someone attractive. The field has been described as suffering from small samples, publication bias, false positives and weak methodology [1].

Advertisers claim body sprays contain human sexual pheromones acting as aphrodisiacs. Wikipedia states that no pheromonal substance has been shown in a peer-reviewed study to directly influence human behaviour and describes the claims as disputed [1].

Scent features in male grooming discussions on forums such as T Nation. One poster in a 2015 thread on fashion says he started wearing cologne because of an expectation that it activates memory centres and has aphrodisiac qualities, which another poster in the same thread questions [4].

No studies found of these commercial products. Spray research located under the term pheromone spray concerns insects such as codling moths, honey bees and carpenter ants [2][3][5]. Human studies of individual putative pheromones are described above [1].
